title: From Anomaly to Action: Connecting Storage Intelligence to Cyber Recovery
summary: Storage anomaly detection becomes recovery intelligence: the Everpure and Commvault workflow connects Pure1, Fusion, and Commvault Cloud Threat Scan.
body_text: Summary Everpure and Commvault connect storage intelligence with workload-aware threat detection and cyber recovery workflows, helping organizations investigate anomalies faster, prioritize risk, and recover with greater confidence. Everpure and Commvault connect storage intelligence with cyber recovery workflows Cyber resilience depends on speed, confidence, and context. When something suspicious happens, teams need more than another alert — they need to understand what may be affected, where to investigate first, and how to move quickly toward recovery without adding risk or complexity. Storage should be part of the defense Storage has long been treated as something organizations need to protect from attackers. But in a modern cyber resilience strategy, storage can do more. It can become part of the defense foundation itself: a source of early signals , recovery context, and operational intelligence that helps teams respond faster when disruption strikes. That’s the idea behind the new Everpure Commvault anomaly workflow. Turning storage anomalies into recovery intelligence The Everpure Commvault anomaly workflow connects Pure1 ® anomaly detection, Everpure Fusion ™ fleet context, and Commvault IntelliSnap metadata to help turn storage-layer anomalies into workload-aware threat and recovery intelligence inside Commvault Cloud . When Pure1 detects anomalous behavior on an Everpure FlashArray™ volume, the workflow identifies affected protected workloads and raises anomaly events for them in Commvault Cloud Threat Scan . In simple terms: Pure1 detects. Everpure Fusion enriches. Commvault operationalizes. Pure1 monitors Everpure storage telemetry and identifies unusual behavior on FlashArray volumes. Everpure Fusion provides the array and fleet context needed to make that signal more actionable. Commvault provides IntelliSnap metadata to help map the anomalous volume to protected clients or virtual machine(VMs)s. The workflow raises anomaly events for those workloads in Commvault Cloud to enrich the threat profiles and help determine the right course of action, from scanning backups to full recovery. This workflow integrates with the Everpure Enterprise Data Cloud framework and Everpure Fusion fleet context, helping extend Everpure storage intelligence into partner cyber resilience workflows. It’s a practical example of how ecosystem integration can turn storage telemetry into useful recovery context inside the tools teams already use to protect, investigate, and recover. Closing the gap between signals and action Storage, backup, and security teams often have strong tools, but those tools can operate in silos. A storage team may see anomalous volume. A backup team may manage protected workloads. A security team may be investigating a potential incident. But manually stitching those signals together is complicated and takes time, and it can mean the difference between identifying a cyber event early enough to minimize the impact and having a massive compromise. The Everpure Commvault anomaly workflow helps reduce that manual burden. Instead of forcing teams to jump between consoles and correlate arrays, volumes, snapshots, jobs, clients, and VMs on their own, the workflow helps bring storage anomaly context into Commvault as an actionable event. That gives teams a faster path from “something unusual happened” to “the risk profile on these workloads just increased.” The result is faster triage, better prioritization, and more informed recovery decisions. Recovery teams gain improved threat analysis, and their recovery workflows can take advantage of FlashArray snapshots to bring compromised workloads back faster. Security and infrastructure teams gain shared context across storage and data protection operations. And organizations gain another way to make storage an active part of the cyber-resilient foundation , not just another target to defend. Designed for IntelliSnap-protected block workloads The initial workflow release is focused on block-based workloads protected with Commvault IntelliSnap. VMs hosted on Everpure systems, including VMware raw device mappings, databases, and file systems, are all supported. Resilience architectures such as failover clusters and array-based replication are included. The workflow works in conjunction with Commvault Cloud Threat Scan to strengthen the workload risk profiles that identify where action is needed and what actions to take, including malware scans of protected data and recovery of impacted systems. Cyber resilience isn’t just about having more alerts. It’s about turning the right signals into the right actions at the right time. With the Everpure Commvault anomaly aorkflow, storage anomalies no longer have to remain isolated infrastructure events. They can become workload-aware threat signals in Commvault Cloud. Together, Everpure and Commvault are helping customers move from t, connecting storage intelligence with cyber recovery workflows so teams can investigate faster, reduce manual effort, and recover with greater confidence. title: When Can LLMs Replace Humans in A/B Tests?
summary: TL;DR: LLM predictions can stand in for human outcomes in A/B tests, but only by assumption, not by design. In an application to the Upworthy dataset with thousands of A/B tests, calibrating LLM outputs against human data recovered the treatment effect, but only using a specific set of methods. The promise is least justified precisely when it offers the most benefit.
body_text: TL;DR: LLM predictions can stand in for human outcomes in A/B tests, but only by assumption, not by design. In an application to the Upworthy dataset with thousands of A/B tests, calibrating LLM outputs against human data recovered the treatment effect, but only using a specific set of methods. The conditions that make this work cannot be verified for new treatments, and they become less plausible the further the new treatment is from past experiments. The promise is least justified precisely when it offers the most benefit. The promise is straightforward: run the experiment on a model instead of on users, get results in hours instead of weeks, and skip the traffic allocation entirely. But most proposals for replacing humans with LLM in A/B tests skip the statistical question that makes experiments valid in the first place: under what conditions does the experiment identify the treatment effect of interest? Randomized experiments are considered the gold-standard because they causally identify the treatment effect by design. Replacing real user responses with LLM-generated predictions removes that guarantee. Identification then holds only by assumption. We wrote a paper that formalizes what those assumptions are, using surrogate endpoint theory from biostatistics. Our idea is simple: If a surrogate outcome captures everything about a treatment that matters for the outcome, then, clearly, the surrogate is a valid proxy and experimenting on it will give the correct result. In clinical trials, biomarkers from labs are commonly used as fast and cheap surrogates for the clinical result. For A/B tests in digital environments, LLM predictions have become attractive candidates as surrogates for user responses. The promise is that LLM predictions sidesteps the effort, time, and opportunity costs of A/B testing. Raw LLM predictions are biased, not just noisy We empirically evaluated the promise of LLM-based A/B testing using the Upworthy Research Archive , the largest open-access dataset on A/B tests currently available. The dataset contains click-through rates for variants of news headlines across thousands of A/B tests. We prompted gpt-4o-mini to predict the click-through rate of a typical user for each headline, separately for the treatment and control variants. Using those raw predictions in a standard experimental analysis recovered only 39% of the observed human treatment effect. If you used those predictions as if they were human data, you would conclude that treatments are less than half as effective as they actually are. This is not just random noise. The bias is systematic and directional: LLM outcomes attenuate treatment effects toward zero, making treatments look less effective than they are. A/B tests are used to learn what users value for making better product decisions. If LLM-based experiments are used across many features and product areas, that attenuation causes the organization to underestimate the value they bring to users, and potentially make incorrect shipping decisions. Two conditions make LLM outputs valid surrogates Our paper formalizes two conditions under which LLM predictions can be used to identify a human average treatment effect. Surrogacy . This assumption requires that the LLM output fully mediates the treatment effect on the human outcome. After accounting for the LLM's prediction and any covariates capturing baseline characteristics independent of treatment, the assignment of a user to the treatment or control condition tells you nothing additional about what the user would do. In plain language: the LLM captures everything about the treatment that matters for the human response. This assumption is often implicitly assumed but rarely spelled out in LLM-based A/B testing, nor is it commonly validated. Fig 1. The surrogacy assumption. LLM predictions fully mediate the treatment effect on humans given covariates. Comparability . This assumption requires that the relationship between LLM predictions and human outcomes, the calibration function , remains the same in the new experiment as in the historical data used to estimate it. If the way LLM predictions map to human behavior shifts when the treatment changes, the calibration breaks. This assumption can be generalized to require that the full distribution over pre-treatment characteristics and LLM predictions is stable across experiments. If satisfied, this allows for identifying not just the average treatment effect but other quantities of the effect distribution. Fig 2. The comparability assumption. The distribution of human outcomes given covariates and the LLM predictions is stable across the human and LLM sample. When both conditions hold, you can calibrate LLM outputs on A/B test data on users to recover the human treatment effect. When either fails, the estimate will be biased. This bias is not because of a lack of data, but because the procedure identifies something else. Thus, even if you generated an infinite number of LLM predictions, the effect on users would not be recovered, but just the effect on the LLM. Unlike random assignment in a user experiment, neither assumption is guaranteed by design. Calibration recovers the effect, but only with the right method Not all calibration methods work equally well. We tested two on the Upworthy data. Linear calibration using ordinary least squares (OLS) failed the falsification test: a statistical test that checks whether the calibrated effects measured on the LLM responses are different from the human effects on experiments that were held out from training. If the null hypothesis of no difference is rejected, we conclude that the calibrated estimator is unreliable for past data and should not be trusted on new data either. In this case, we found that linear calibration fitted with OLS was too rigid to capture how LLM predictions map to human behavior, landing 3.8 standard errors from the human benchmark. Machine learning models (random forest and gradient-boosted trees) worked better. For these methods, the calibrated estimate fell within the sampling error of the human effect and was thus not statistically significant. These machine learning models were therefore flexible enough to learn the nonlinear relationship between LLM predictions and human outcomes, thereby calibrating the LLM predictions appropriately. A separate problem is that a single LLM prediction is noisy because of sampling temperature (the randomness in token generation). Unless accounted for, this randomness inherent to LLMs will tend to bias the effect estimate to zero and increase its variance. In our paper, we draw upon measurement error theory and show that simply drawing several outputs from the LLM per experimental unit and using the average as the new LLM prediction mitigates this problem. Intuitively, this stems from the noise component in the LLM predictions is then averaged out, leaving what's left to be closer to the true signal. The real limitation is about future interventions The surrogacy and comparability conditions can be partially assessed on historical data. They can never be proved to hold for a treatment you have never tested before. This is a central constraint. The further a new treatment departs from what you have tested before, the weaker the basis for trusting the LLM output as a valid stand-in for human responses. For genuinely new interventions, such as a different UI paradigm, a new pricing model, a feature unlike anything you have shipped, the assumptions are inherently untestable. That is, the setting in which LLMs offer the most benefit for A/B testing is precisely where they are least likely to work. Human experiments therefore remain indispensable for true product innovation. Against this background, it should be noted that the Upworthy dataset is a near-ideal test case for LLM surrogacy. The outcome is binary (click or not), the treatments are text-based and linguistically similar (headline variants), and LLMs are trained on vast amounts of text about what makes headlines engaging. For treatments that change layouts, algorithms, or pricing, the necessary conditions for LLM-based A/B testing are harder to justify. There is no empirical evidence that the conditions hold in general, for instance, across a company's portfolio of innovations, as would be required to use it at scale. Calibration needs the data you are trying to avoid collecting Our work shows that LLM-based A/B testing can, in theory, work, but requires strong assumptions to hold, careful and context-dependent application of methods, and thorough validation. The Upworthy dataset includes thousands of past experiments of a single type. Most product teams instead have a diverse collection of experiments from different surfaces and product areas, which may even come with different logging. The framework does not eliminate the need for user experiments; it shows that you can only reduce how many user experiments you need when the new experiments resemble ones already run, by letting extrapolation fill in the gap. The upfront investment in collecting actual user responses is not optional, but is what makes LLM-based A/B testing trustworthy. Changes in LLMs add further complications. Any calibration function is fit to a specific model at a specific point in time. Providers of LLMs update and replace models. A calibration function learned today may not be valid six months from now, even for the same model. Moreover, any new calibration function should ideally be fitted on new user experiments, as otherwise it may be temporally biased. Even if surrogacy and comparability can be made more realistic over time, for instance through better LLMs, prompting or fine-tuning, one still needs to run user experiments to calibrate the LLM outputs, or check that they indeed do map to user outcomes. Advances in LLM predictions is not a way out of human validation. Final words: User experiments work by design, LLM-based experiments by assumption The surrogacy framework considers when an LLM prediction is a valid proxy metric for human behavior. Like all proxy metrics, LLM surrogates work until the relationship between proxy and outcome shifts. The framework makes that relationship explicit, testable, and highlights its consequences when it fails. It cannot guarantee the relationship holds for the experiment you care about most: the one testing something new. That said, LLM predictions can make human experiments better. They can be used to filter out weak ideas before they consume an experiment slot, or serve as covariates for variance reduction . They thereby offer improvements to experimental selection and efficiency when you have strong historical data and the new treatment resembles past ones. Substituting them for human outcomes is a different move. It trades identification by design for identification by assumption. Do not give that up. Tags: Data Science SHARE THIS ARTICLE

title: How to Send Wedding Thank You Notes: Timeline, Etiquette & Wording Examples
summary: Every wedding gift deserves a genuine, handwritten thank you — and every couple needs a plan to actually get them sent. This guide covers who needs a
body_text: Last Updated on August 3, 2026 by Joy Editors Every wedding gift deserves a genuine, handwritten thank you — and every couple needs a plan to actually get them sent. This guide covers who needs a note, when to send it, what to write for every scenario, and how to stay organized so nothing slips through the cracks. At the end, we will show you how Joy can help you manage the entire process from one dashboard. Quick answer: A good wedding thank you note is 3–5 sentences. Mention the person by name, reference the specific gift, share how you plan to use it, and close with a warm sign-off. Send all notes within three months of your wedding — aim for eight weeks after returning from your honeymoon. Use a gift tracker to keep track of who gave what so nobody gets missed. Who Needs a Thank You Note? The short answer: anyone who gave you something — a physical gift, cash, a cash fund contribution, or even their time and travel. Here is a quick breakdown: Every guest who gave a gift — whether they attended the wedding or not. Cash fund contributors — even small contributions deserve a personal note. Group gift contributors — each person gets their own individual note, not one card for the group. Wedding party members — bridesmaids, groomsmen, maid of honor, best man. They gave time, money, and emotional support. Parents and close family — especially those who contributed financially or helped plan. Guests who traveled — acknowledge the effort even if they did not give a separate gift. Coworkers, your boss, neighbors, and family friends — anyone who sent a gift or made a meaningful gesture. Virtual wedding attendees — they showed up from afar, and that counts. Vendors (optional) — photographers, planners, and caterers who went above and beyond appreciate a kind note. If you are unsure whether someone needs a note, err on the side of sending one. A brief, genuine message is always welcome. Wedding Thank You Note Timeline Timing matters. A prompt note feels thoughtful; a late one can feel like an afterthought. Here is the timeline to follow: Pre-wedding gifts (shower gifts, early registry purchases): Send a thank you within two weeks of receiving the gift. Wedding day gifts and cards: Send within one month of returning from your honeymoon. Cash fund and registry gifts: Send within eight weeks post-honeymoon. Firm deadline: All notes should be sent within three months of your wedding date. Running late? A late note is always better than no note. Acknowledge the delay briefly and move on — do not over-apologize. Pro tip: Set a weekly goal instead of trying to write everything at once. Ten notes per sitting keeps the quality high and the task manageable. Wedding Thank You Note Wording for Registry Gifts Registry gifts are the easiest to write because you already know what the person gave. Mention the item by name and say something genuine about how you will use it. Template 1 — Kitchen or home item: Dear [Name], Thank you so much for the [item]. We have already put it to good use — [brief personal detail, e.g., “made our first Sunday breakfast with it”]. Your thoughtfulness means so much to us, and we are so glad you were there to celebrate with us. With love, [Your Names] Template 2 — Decor or keepsake: Dear [Name], The [item] is absolutely beautiful. We have found the perfect spot for it in our [room], and it will always remind us of this time in our lives. Thank you for celebrating with us and for your generosity. Warmly, [Your Names] Wedding Thank You Note Wording for Money or Cash Gifts When someone gives cash or a check, do not mention the dollar amount. Instead, share what you plan to do with it. This keeps the note personal and avoids any awkwardness. Template 1 — General cash gift: Dear [Name], Thank you so much for your generous gift. We are putting it toward [honeymoon / new home / a piece of furniture we have had our eye on], and it will make such a difference. We are so grateful for your support and love. With love, [Your Names] Template 2 — Honeymoon fund contribution: Dear [Name], Thank you for contributing to our honeymoon fund. Because of you, we got to [experience / upgrade to / enjoy] [specific detail, e.g., “a sunset dinner cruise in Santorini”]. It was a memory we will carry with us always. We are so lucky to have you in our lives. Love, [Your Names] If you used a cash fund on your wedding website , you can see exactly who contributed and how much, which makes personalizing these notes much easier. Wedding Thank You Note Wording for Money or Cash Gifts When someone gives cash or a check, do not mention the dollar amount. Instead, share what you plan to do with it. This keeps the note personal and avoids any awkwardness. Template 1 — General cash gift: Dear [Name], Thank you so much for your generous gift. We are putting it toward [honeymoon / new home / a piece of furniture we have had our eye on], and it will make such a difference. We are so grateful for your support and love. With love, [Your Names] Template 2 — Honeymoon fund contribution: Dear [Name], Thank you for contributing to our honeymoon fund. Because of you, we got to [experience / upgrade to / enjoy] [specific detail, e.g., “a sunset dinner cruise in Santorini”]. It was a memory we will carry with us always. We are so lucky to have you in our lives. Love, [Your Names] Wedding Thank You Note Wording for People Who Traveled Guests who traveled a significant distance to attend deserve a note that acknowledges the effort, even if they also gave a gift. Template — Guest who traveled to attend: Dear [Name], Thank you so much for making the trip from [city] to celebrate with us. Knowing you were in the room made the day feel complete. We hope the journey was worth it — we certainly think it was. We cannot wait to see you again soon. With love, [Your Names] Wedding Thank You Note Wording for Wedding Party Members Your wedding party gave time, money, and energy. Their notes should reflect that. Reference something specific they did during the planning process or on the day itself. Template — Maid of honor or best man: Dear [Name], There are not enough words to thank you for everything you did leading up to and on our wedding day. From [specific moment, e.g., “organizing the rehearsal dinner”] to keeping me calm when I needed it most, you were everything I could have asked for. Thank you for your friendship and for making our day so special. With so much love, [Your Name] Template — Bridesmaid or groomsman: Dear [Name], Thank you for standing beside us on one of the most important days of our lives. Your support throughout this whole process has meant the world to us. We are so grateful to have you as a friend, and we cannot wait to celebrate many more milestones together. Love, [Your Names] Wedding Thank You Note Wording for Parents Parent notes are the most personal of all. These are the people who raised you, helped fund the wedding, or simply showed up in every way that mattered. Take a few extra minutes on these. Template — Parents: Dear [Mom and Dad / Name], Thank you for everything you did to make our wedding day possible. From [specific contribution, e.g., “the flowers you arranged” or “the way you welcomed [Partner] into our family”], your love and generosity shaped every part of this celebration. We are so grateful for you, and we love you more than we can say. All our love, [Your Names] Wedding Thank You Note Wording for Coworkers, Your Boss, and Neighbors Professional and community relationships call for a warm but slightly more polished tone. Keep things genuine without being overly casual. Template — Coworker: Dear [Name], Thank you so much for the [gift]. It was such a thoughtful surprise, and it means a lot to know you were thinking of us. We are lucky to have such kind people in our work lives. Thank you for the well wishes and generosity. Warmly, [Your Names] Template — Boss or manager: Dear [Name], Thank you for the [gift] and for all the kind words and support during the wedding planning process. Your generosity and flexibility meant more than you know. We truly appreciate it. With gratitude, [Your Names] Template — Neighbor: Dear [Name], Thank you so much for the [gift / kind gesture]. Having such wonderful neighbors makes everything better — and your thoughtfulness around our wedding was no exception. We are so grateful for your support. With love, [Your Names] Wedding Thank You Note Wording for Virtual Wedding Attendees Guests who attended virtually still showed up — and that effort deserves a note, especially if they also sent a gift. Template — Virtual guest: Dear [Name], Thank you so much for joining us virtually on our wedding day. Even though we were not in the same room, knowing you were watching and celebrating with us from [city / home] meant the world. [If they sent a gift: “And thank you for the [gift] — we love it.”] We hope to celebrate together in person soon. With love, [Your Names] Wedding Thank You Note Wording for a Group Gift When multiple guests chip in on one gift, send each person their own individual note. Do not send a single group card — it feels impersonal. Dear [Name], Thank you so much for contributing to the [item]. We were so touched that you and [names of others] came together on such a generous gift. We have been enjoying it ever since and think of all of you every time we use it. Thank you for your thoughtfulness and for celebrating with us. With love, [Your Names] Wedding Thank You Note Wording for Someone Who Could Not Attend If someone sent a gift but could not make it to the wedding, acknowledge their absence warmly. Do not make them feel bad about missing it. Dear [Name], Thank you so much for the [gift] and for thinking of us even though you could not be there. We missed having you with us, but knowing you were celebrating from afar meant a great deal. We hope to see you soon and celebrate together in person. With love, [Your Names] Wedding Thank You Note Wording for Vendors Sending a note to your vendors is not required, but it is a thoughtful gesture — especially for photographers, planners, and caterers who put real care into their work. Dear [Vendor Name], Thank you for the incredible work you did at our wedding. [Specific detail, e.g., “The photos captured everything we hoped for and more.” or “The food was the highlight of the reception for so many of our guests.”] We are so glad we found you, and we will be recommending you to everyone we know. With gratitude, With love, [Your Names] Wedding Thank You Note Wording for a Late Note Sending a late note is always better than not sending one at all. Acknowledge the delay briefly, then move on. Do not over-apologize. Dear [Name], We owe you a long-overdue thank you for the [gift]. Life after the wedding moved faster than we expected, but please know your generosity was not forgotten. We truly appreciate your kindness and your support throughout this whole chapter of our lives. With love, [Your Names] Wedding Thank You Note Etiquette: The Key Rules Timeline: Send notes within three months of your wedding date. Aim for eight weeks post-honeymoon as your personal deadline. Handwritten vs. printed: Handwritten is always the right choice for wedding thank you notes. Printed cards feel impersonal for this occasion. Both names: If you are married, both names should appear in the sign-off, even if only one person writes the notes. Specific over generic: “Thank you for the gift” is not enough. Name the item or gesture. This is the single most important rule. Length: Three to five sentences is ideal. Longer is not always better. Do not mention dollar amounts: For cash gifts, never write the amount. Reference what you plan to do with it instead. Common Thank You Note Mistakes to Avoid Even well-intentioned couples stumble on these. Here are the most common mistakes — and how to sidestep them: Using a generic template without personalizing it. Every note should mention the specific gift and include at least one personal detail. Guests can tell when they received a copy-paste. Mentioning dollar amounts for cash gifts. Never write the amount. Say what you plan to do with it instead. Sending one group note for a group gift. Each contributor gets their own note. Always. Waiting too long to start. The longer you wait, the harder it gets. Start writing within a week of returning from your honeymoon. Forgetting guests who did not give a physical gift. People who traveled, attended virtually, or were part of the wedding party still deserve a note. Over-apologizing in a late note. One brief acknowledgment is enough. Spending half the note apologizing dilutes the gratitude. Skipping the note because you thanked them in person. A verbal thank you at the reception is great, but it does not replace a written note. Not tracking who gave what. Without a system, gifts get mixed up and people get missed. Use a gift tracker from day one. How to Stay Organized With Your Wedding Thank You Notes The biggest challenge is not writing the notes — it is keeping track of who gave what. Here is how to stay on top of it: Track gifts as they arrive. Do not wait until after the wedding. Log every gift — registry items, cash, checks, group contributions — the moment it shows up. The longer you wait, the harder it is to remember who sent what. Verify mailing addresses. Before you start writing, make sure you have a current address for each recipient. Wedding address books get outdated fast, and returned mail means a delayed thank you. Your guest list manager can help you keep addresses in one place. Track cash fund contributions. Cash fund gifts are easy to lose track of because there is no physical item to jog your memory. If you used a cash fund through Joy , every contribution is logged with the guest’s name and amount — so you never have to wonder who contributed. Batch your writing sessions. Write ten notes per sitting rather than trying to finish everything at once. The quality stays higher and the task feels less overwhelming. Mark each note as sent. Use your gift tracker to check off completed notes so you can see at a glance what is left. How Joy Helps You Manage Thank You Notes If you planned your wedding with Joy , your thank you note process is already half done. Joy’s built-in gift tracker logs every registry purchase and cash fund contribution automatically, so you always know who gave what. From your gift tracker , you can compose and send digital thank you notes directly to your guests’ inboxes — Joy even generates a first draft based on the gift details. You can edit the wording, update the subject line, add a photo from your wedding, and preview the message before sending. It is the fastest way to make sure every guest feels appreciated without losing track of a single gift. For couples who prefer handwritten notes, the gift tracker still serves as your master list. Filter by gift type, check off notes as you send them, and export addresses when you need them. Frequently Asked Questions How long do you have to send wedding thank you notes? The traditional guideline is within three months of your wedding date. Most etiquette experts recommend sending notes within eight weeks of returning from your honeymoon. Sending late is always better than not sending at all. What should you write in a wedding thank you note for money? Do not mention the dollar amount. Instead, share what you plan to do with the gift — whether that is contributing to your honeymoon, a new home, or a specific purchase. This keeps the note personal and avoids any awkwardness around amounts. Do you have to send thank you notes to everyone at your wedding? Yes. Anyone who gave a gift — whether they attended or not — should receive a thank you note. For guests who attended but did not give a gift, a note is a kind gesture but not required. Vendors who went above and beyond also appreciate a note. Can wedding thank you notes be typed or printed? Handwritten notes are strongly preferred for wedding thank yous. Printed cards feel impersonal for this occasion. If your handwriting is difficult to read, write slowly and clearly — the effort matters more than perfect penmanship. Can you send thank you notes digitally? Yes — digital thank you notes are becoming more common, especially for cash fund contributions and guests who attended virtually. Joy lets you send personalized digital thank you notes directly from your gift tracker, complete with a custom message and wedding photo. Should you send a thank you note to someone who attended but did not give a gift? It is not strictly required, but it is a kind gesture — especially if the guest traveled a long distance or was part of your wedding party. A brief note acknowledging their presence and support is always appreciated.

title: AR collections software: 7 tools to help crush DSO targets
summary: Discover 7 AR collections software to get paid faster. Compare platforms on features, pricing, and true AI capabilities.
body_text: At this very minute, roughly 40 percent of invoices in the US alone are overdue. The finance teams that recover that cash fastest aren't actually working harder . So what's their secret? They've stopped chasing invoices by hand and handed the repetitive parts to AI-powered AR collections software. The right AR collections software tracks every open invoice, follows up on your cadence, reads what customers write back, and tells you exactly where your money is, so your team spends its time on the accounts that actually need (human) attention. In this guide, we compare seven AR collection software platforms worth evaluating in 2026: Alguna, Fazeshift, Stuut, Paraglide, Upflow, Zenskar, and Tabs. We'll walk through what each one does well, where it falls short, and how to pick the right fit for your business. If you've already done your research and want to see Alguna in action, book your personalized demo . What is AR collections software? ℹ️ AR collections software is a category of tools that automates the work of collecting money your customers owe you . It covers invoice tracking, payment reminders, follow-up on overdue accounts, cash application, and reporting on metrics like days sales outstanding (DSO). Some people call it AR collection management software or AR collection tracking software. The job is the same: get invoices paid sooner with less manual effort. It sits alongside, and often overlaps with, broader accounts receivable software . The difference is emphasis. General AR software manages the full receivables ledger. AR collections software focuses on the collections motion specifically: who owes you, how overdue they are, what you've said to them, and what happens next. Here's what a modern AR collections software process usually looks like once it's set up: Invoice tracking. Every open invoice lands in one place, sorted by aging bucket, customer, and amount, so nothing slips through the cracks. Automated follow-ups. The software sends reminders on a cadence you define, anchored to the invoice date, due date, or last action, instead of someone copy-pasting the same email 40 times a week. Reply handling. The better platforms read what customers send back, capture promises to pay, and pause outreach when a dispute comes up. Cash application. Incoming payments get matched to the right invoices, so your books stay accurate without manual reconciliation. Reporting. Live dashboards show outstanding cash, DSO, and which accounts need attention, so finance leaders can act on real numbers. The newest wave of AR collections automation software goes further than scheduled reminders. Tools built on autonomous AR agents read replies, understand context, and work your aging with very little hand-holding. We'll flag which platforms below do that and which are closer to smart automation. AR collections software compared at a glance Here's a high-level view before we go deep on each platform. How to evaluate AR collections software Choosing the right tool isn't about the longest feature list. Here's what actually moves the needle. Real AI versus scheduled reminders. A lot of platforms use "AI" to describe what is functionally a timed reminder sequence. The distinction matters. Does the tool read customer replies and respond to them? Does it capture promises to pay and pause outreach accordingly? Does it handle disputes without a human stepping in? Ask every vendor to demo exactly how their platform handles a customer reply. Cash application depth. Matching incoming payments to open invoices is where a lot of manual time disappears. Ask how the platform handles partial payments, consolidated remittances, and parent-child account hierarchies. This is the heart of any serious cash application workflow. Controls and guardrails. If the platform uses AI agents for outreach, you need to know how much control you keep. Look for configurable autonomy levels, approval thresholds tied to invoice amounts, and hard guardrails that stop the agent from making legal threats, offering discounts, or admitting fault. Alguna's autonomy ladder is a useful model to benchmark against. Billing model fit. If you run usage-based, hybrid, or custom pricing, plenty of AR tools will struggle. Make sure the platform can ingest your usage data, generate accurate invoices from it, and handle mid-period changes. Integrations that fit your stack. Your AR software has to connect to your CRM, billing system, and ERP without manual exports. Check for native integrations, not Zapier workarounds, with the systems you already run. If you're on Salesforce and NetSuite, or QuickBooks Online, or Sage Intacct, confirm those specific connectors exist and how deep they go. Implementation and migration. The biggest risk in switching financial software is the migration. Ask how long it takes, who does the heavy lifting, and what data migration involves. A hands-on process cuts risk, so ask for references from teams that moved from a setup like yours. For a deeper look at agent-led collections specifically, our guide to intelligent collections breaks down what separates genuine automation from dressed-up reminders. Frequently asked questions about AR collections software How does AI-driven AR collection software match payments to invoices? AI-driven AR collection software matches payments to invoices by reading incoming remittance data, parsing amounts and references, and reconciling each payment against your open invoices in the ERP, including partial payments and consolidated remittances. The stronger platforms post the matched cash to the ledger automatically and flag only the exceptions that need a human, which is what turns cash application from a daily chore into a background process. Which AR collection software integrates with Salesforce and NetSuite? If you need AR collection software that integrates with Salesforce and NetSuite, Alguna, Fazeshift, and Zenskar all connect to both, and Upflow integrates with NetSuite. Alguna offers native Salesforce and general ledger connections alongside its AR Agent, so collections data stays in sync with your CRM and accounting records without manual exports. Always confirm the depth of each connector, since a native two-way sync is very different from a one-directional feed. Can you automate collection letters with AR software? Yes. Every platform in this guide can automate collection letters and reminders on a cadence you define. The difference is what happens after the letter goes out. Basic tools send the next scheduled message regardless of context, while agent-based tools like Alguna and Stuut read the reply, capture a promise to pay, pause on a dispute, and adjust the next step based on what the customer actually said. What's the best AR collection software for multiple subsidiaries? For the best AR collection software for multiple subsidiaries, look for multi-entity and multi-currency support, consolidated reporting across entities, and cash application that handles parent-child account hierarchies. Alguna supports multi-currency collections across a connected revenue platform, and enterprise-focused tools like Fazeshift are built for parent-child hierarchies and multi-entity operations. Confirm during the demo that each subsidiary can run its own cadences and personas while rolling up into one view. What's the best payment collection and AR software for QuickBooks Online users? For QuickBooks Online users, the best payment collection and AR software is one that offers a native, two-way QuickBooks integration so invoices and payments stay in sync. Alguna, Upflow, Zenskar, and Tabs all integrate with QuickBooks. What's the best payment collection and AR software for Sage Intacct users? For Sage Intacct users, look for AR software with a proven Sage Intacct connector that syncs invoices, payments, and cash application. Fazeshift and Tabs both integrate with Sage Intacct, and Fazeshift's contract agent can set up invoicing directly in it. Ask each vendor how the connector handles cash posting back to Sage Intacct, since that's where reconciliation work usually piles up. What's the difference between AR collections software and billing software? Billing software generates and sends invoices. AR collections software manages what happens after the invoice is sent: tracking payments, following up on overdue accounts, and reconciling cash. Some platforms, like Alguna and Zenskar, cover both in one workflow, which removes the data handoff between billing and collections that causes most accuracy problems. If you want the full picture, see our roundup of accounts receivable AI software and our primer on the accounts receivable AI agent . Stop letting earned cash sit overdue The gap between the finance teams that get paid on time and the ones that don't isn't about effort anymore. It's about tooling. title: Emotion Leads CX Quality Rebound In The US
summary: Customer experience quality has improved.
body_text: After four years of decline, customer experience (CX) in the United States has finally ticked back upward. New findings from Forrester’s 2026 Customer Experience Index (CX Index™) reveal a modest but important improvement in overall CX quality, marking the first year-over-year increase since 2021. At the same time, the data shows that organizations still have major ground to regain before returning to pre-decline performance levels. A closer look at the three underlying dimensions of CX performance — effectiveness, ease, and emotion — reveals encouraging news. In 2026, performance improved on each of these quality metrics, contributing to the rise in overall CX performance. Of the three dimensions, emotional quality had the largest gain, increasing by 1.4 percentage points year over year. This result is significant because emotion is often the strongest predictor of customer loyalty, advocacy, and retention and often the most difficult to improve. More Brands Have Improved This year’s uptick is notable not only because average scores increased but also because improvement became more common at the brand level. Among the 225 brands we evaluated in both 2025 and 2026, 26% achieved statistically significant improvements while just 7% had statistically significant declines. The percent age s of brands that improved and declined in 2026 are nearly the opposite of the percentages in 2025, signaling a meaningful shift in momentum. Continued Progress Is Possible Despite this encouraging news, leaders should be cautious about declaring victory. Overall CX Index scores and individual-quality dimension performance all remain slightly below their 2024 levels, and sustained progress over multiple years will be needed to confirm that the long-term decline in CX quality has truly been reversed. On the other hand, this uptick shows that improving CX is possible even in challenging business environments. Organizations that focus on delivering more effective interactions, reducing customer effort, and strengthening emotional connections can generate measurable gains. Continued investment and discipline can continue the momentum. And don’t forget the other components of the total experience that can drive growth for your organization: brand experience and employee experience . Forrester clients can further explore brand- and industry-level results from Forrester’s CX Index and discuss its role in the total experience by scheduling a guidance session with me . Share

title: How long does the seller have to respond to an offer on a house?
summary: How long does a seller have to respond to an offer on a house? Understand why delays happen, key signs of acceptance, and ways to make your offer stronger.
body_text: Preparing to make an offer on a home that's for sale? It’s natural to wonder: How long does a seller have to respond to an offer on a house? For that matter, how long does the seller have to accept an offer, and does a seller have to respond to an offer at all? Truth is, sellers may not be required to meet a particular buyer response deadline (depending on what is specified in the purchase agreement), and they are not legally required to respond at all. Learn more about what’s involved with accepting an offer on a house and associated timelines, why the seller may not respond to your offer, what to do if the seller is unresponsive, signs your offer will be accepted, and how you can make your offer more attractive . How long does a seller have to accept an offer? When you make an offer on a listed property, the seller is allowed to take as much time as they want to accept or respond– unless you have indicated a deadline in your offer. “In reality, the majority of offers made by buyers include a listed expiration date – often between 24 and 72 hours. This gives the negotiations structure and keeps them from going on forever,” says Dennis Shirshikov , a professor of financeand economics at City University of New York/Queens College. Many purchase agreements presented by the buyer to the seller include a default response time. “In our Los Angeles market, that default response time is typically three days,” explains Martin Feinberg , a Realtor/broker with Keller Williams. “However, if a buyer is submitting what they feel is an aggressive offer that’s better than asking price on a property that has high interest and activity, they will often ask for a response within 24 to 36 hours.” See your homebuying budget ...in as little as 3 minutes – no credit impact Does a seller have to respond to an offer? Contrary to the belief of some buyers, the seller is not legally required to respond to any offer. If your offer doesn’t meet their standards, or if they receive better offers, they may choose to ignore or reject your offer. “That being said, it’s a matter of professional etiquette for the seller’s agent to communicate to the buyer the seller’s decision,” notes Elizabeth Powers , a Realtor with Christie’s International Real Estate Sereno. Why is the seller not responding to your offer? There are common reasons why a home seller may ignore your offer without a response: Your offer was too low. They have multiple/better offers. The seller is skeptical about your offer. “If your offer is significantly less than the asking price, if the seller has several competing offers to consider, or if the seller has concerns about your ability to finance the purchase and afford the loan and the monthly payments , they may choose to remain silent,” Shirshikov continues. “Silence itself is occasionally employed as a negotiating strategy to convey indifference.” In Feinberg’s experience, typically, when a seller opts not to respond to your offer, it’s due to the buyer’s price being too low to merit a counteroffer. “Or, in some cases, you may be taking an offer that’s contingent on the sale of your property – which most sellers won’t consider,” he says. Not all rejected offers look the same Be aware that purchase agreements include a section in which the listing agent and/or seller can indicate “rejected.” Feinberg points out that this isn’t always utilized, but in some cases, the buyer prefers that in writing to prove that the seller did, in fact, review their offer and that the listing agent didn’t act independently in rejecting your offer. “Sellers' agents are legally required to present all written offers to their seller clients, although presentation can be verbal as well as providing a buyer’s actual written offer,” adds Feinberg. Rick Bannon , a real estate advisor with ONE Sotheby’s International Realty, lists a few other reasons why sellers may not respond to offers. “Perhaps the seller is not financially capable of moving forward without some kind of requirement, such as the need to sell a different house that hasn’t even been listed yet,” says Bannon. “Or maybe they are waiting on an inheritance, or they want an extremely long closing period.” A preapproval can sweeten an offer Another factor that can increase the risk of your offer being ignored? Not including a mortgage loan preapproval letter in your offer. “As a buyer, presenting that approval letter from a reputable lender is the most important step at this stage in the process,” suggests Kerry Adams with Compass Real Estate. Better's AI-driven preapproval can show results within three minutes. Start your preapproval ...in as little as 3 minutes – no credit impact What to do if the seller is not responding If you’ve made an offer that’s only generated silence from the seller, regroup quickly with your real estate agent/Realtorand ask them how to best proceed . “Both your Realtor and the listing agent will have to talk things through and figure out how to get matters moving forward,” says Bannon. “A good real estate agent will ask you to start thinking about what your second and third choices might be at this stage.” Practice patience during this waiting period. Perhaps the seller is away or indisposed; or maybe they just need a bit more time to review your offer and make a decision. Still no reply? Give thought to sweetening the deal by improving your offer. Discuss the pros and cons of this strategy with your agent first. Signs your offer will be accepted If the seller responds to your offer in some way, even if it’s not an immediate acceptance of your offer, it’s likely a good signal that a deal agreement is forthcoming. “Positive indicators include a prompt counteroffer from the seller, a request for additional supporting documentation – such as proof of funds – or inquiries regarding timing. Genuine interest is frequently indicated by sellers who request small changes rather than dismissing an offer outright or ignoring it,” Shirshikov says. Additionally, conversations initiated by the listing agent with your agent can signify a green flag after your purchase contract offer is presented. “If you are in a multiple offer situation, prompt responses from the seller can also be beneficial, but not a guarantee,” says Powers. Set an expiration on your offer To increase the likelihood of the seller responding to your offer, you might want to set an offer expiration date. With a shorter timeline and indicated expiration date, the seller cannot use your offer as leverage while seeking higher bids from other shoppers. “By requiring a decision within a specified window – even if it results in a rejection – it grants you more control,” advises Shirshikov. Powers says she often sees buyer offers that specify a 24- to 48-hour expiration date, which can be particularly useful to buyers who are considering two different homes for sale. However, if the seller has clearly stated that they will not look at offers until a later date, “setting a deadline date on your offer could backfire – especially if you present a low offer,” cautions Adams. “If you plan to include a deadline, talk to your real estate agent about how to make your offer strong enough for the seller to shut the door on other potential buyers.” How can you make your offer more attractive? You can impress the seller and thereby increase the chances of your offer being accepted if you provide: A higher offer as close to the asking price as possible. Flexible closing dates. Proof of funds. A mortgage loan pre-approval letter from a lender. “Even better, furnish a lender letter that indicates you already have underwriting approval,” recommends Feinberg. Fewer contingencies in your offer. A substantial earnest money deposit. “Indicate in your offer that you agree to release your earnest money deposit to the seller upon acceptance of the offer, which can help you prevail when other strong offers are on the table,” Feinberg continues. A larger down payment. “Putting down more money can help the seller feel better about your offer,” says Powers. An all-cash offer. “If you are financially capable, a cash offer always supersedes a finance offer simply because it removes the possibility that the house might not appraise at the contract price or that financing could fall apart before closing,” Bannon notes. A personal letter written to the seller that explains your enthusiasm about buying their home. Seller responding to offer FAQs Is it normal for sellers to accept their first offer? Whether or not the seller will accept the first offer they receive will depend on market conditions, how the offer is structured, and if it meets their needs. Although sellers typically wait for several offers in a competitive market, a well-priced first offer could be accepted quickly in a slower market. What happens after an offer is submitted? The seller and their listing agent have the option to accept, reject, or submit a counter offer once your offer has been submitted. Their agent will review all the terms, check on your qualifications, and make recommendations to the sellerabout how to respond. If your contract offer is accepted, the house will go under contract, after which time an appraisaland (optional) home inspection are conducted, the lender provides an underwriting decision, and the closing commences. Can a seller back out once an offer is accepted? Unless there are special circumstances or a kick-out clause is included in the contract, sellers are typically not allowed to back out of a contract once it has been signed without incurring penalties. They could face financial and legal repercussions if they accept the offer but withdraw without a worthy explanation. The bottom line When you make an offer on a home, be prepared for what happens next. Typically, the seller generally controls the timeline unless you set a clear expiration date in your offer. While sellers are not legally obligated to respond – and “sellernot responding to offer” situations are common – understanding why this happens, how to strengthen your buyer offer, and what steps to take if there’s silence can help you stay proactive and improve your chances of success. See your homebuying budget ...in as little as 3 minutes – no credit impact

title: What’s New: Run multi-modal evaluations end-to-end, smart participant filtering, and more
summary: Video is live in Prolific's AI Task Builder — run text, image, audio and video evaluations end to end, plus smarter participant targeting. See what's new
body_text: From building multimodal evaluations in Prolific to a much slicker way to manage your filter sets, this month's updates make it easier to run precise, high-quality studies. Scroll down to explore what's new. Video is here: run every multimodal eval on Prolific Video is now live in AI Task Builder , which means you can handles the full range of multimodal evaluations end to end with Prolific. Recruit verified participants and run your text, image, audio or video study in a single workflow. Every media type, one task. Present any combination of text, image, audio and video in a single item. Video renders as a native player (play, pause, seek), right alongside your evaluation questions. Side-by-side comparisons for preference evals. Use the configurable two-column layout to put Video / Image A next to Video / Image B for pairwise evals, or RLHF-style preference judgements. Ask questions against each item as participants compare, then collapse into summary questions about the pair (which is better overall, how confident and why). Available in the API and CLI first, coming soon to the UI! Streamlined flow. Split a task into distinct pages so you can build a clear flow for participants, complete with an outro once the task is done. Drop images into your task guidance too: screenshots, scoring rubrics, anything that helps participants understand exactly what to do. Higher participant comprehension means higher quality data. Real responses at API speed. Describe your evaluation and our API handles the rest for you: targeted recruitment from 300,000+ verified participants, study execution and delivery, with a median time to first response of just 4 minutes. Build it into your pipeline via the API or CLI, so no need to tool switch. Get started All live now, you can build multimodal studies directly in the UI , or via the API and CLI to drop them straight into your pipeline. Not sure where to start? Talk to our team and we'll set your first multimodal study up with you. More granular participant recruitment When you need to target a niche audience, you often have to combine multiple conditions at once, for example if you need participants who are employed full-time or part-time, and within a certain age range. Now, you can build more complex queries more easily, with up to 5 OR branches in your filter set. This gives you the flexibility to define exactly the audience you need without compromising on precision or efficiency. Explore in platform or via the API . A smoother filter set experience Reusing and managing your saved audiences is now much easier too: Search for your filter set and view the participant count: Quickly find the set you're after, and see the eligible participant count for each one, so you immediately know whether it'll fill your study. Created by and created date columns: See who created a filter set and when, sorted newest first by default, useful if you reuse filter sets often or share across teams. Rename filter sets: Rename or delete a filter set directly from its detail page. Descriptions: Add an optional description to any filter set, so your team knows exactly what it's for and when to reuse it, which cuts down on guesswork or duplicate sets. Take a look in the UI and the API . Reach the right participants, faster Our Network holds strong at 295,000 90-day active participants. During summer, the smartest way to keep studies filling quickly is to target the right way. Take a look at our quick tips to optimise your participant recruitment: Filter by language, not just country If you need English speakers, narrowing to a single country like the US or UK limits you to a slice of the people who'd qualify. Instead, use the language fluency filter and select ‘English’ to reach 267,000+ active, fluent English speakers across more countries to get the same fluency from a much wider pool. The same trick works well beyond English: language filters reach fluent participants wherever they are. Audiences ready for your next study Some of our deepest pools are wide open right now, so studies targeting them fill fast: South African participants: a sizeable, active pool with plenty of availability Verified Spanish and Dutch speakers: thousands of active language Experts, ideal for localised or language-specific studies. One verified Expert Network Our Expert Network now spans 90,000+ verified Experts across language, healthcare and coding, each individually verified for their skills or credentials. This month brings fresh depth in emerging languages like Thai and Punjabi, alongside established pools such as German (1,470+) and Mandarin (1,130+). Not sure who's on Prolific? Use our Audience Finder to check your audience, or find specialists in-app under Participants > Add screeners > Domain Experts . To find them under the API, take a look here . Watch: The latest episodes in the Frontier Series In our Frontier Series , we interview frontline AI researchers who build the systems, run the studies and explore the questions that don't yet have clean answers. Catch up on the latest episodes recorded at this year’s ICLR: Episode 4: LLM Training as Lossy Compression Prolific's Nora Petrova and John Burden sit down with Henry Conklin (Princeton/Cohere) and Tom Hosking (Cohere), to unpack their paper on treating LLM training as a form of lossy compression . They dig into the two-phase pattern they observed across model sizes during training, and why smaller models may fundamentally struggle to compress enough to generalise well. Watch Episode 4 Episode 5: Inside the Evaluation Problem The conversation continues with Henry and Tom exploring what their compression framing means for evaluation: why compression quality might be a more meaningful signal than benchmark scores, and what that implies for how we train, evaluate and select models going forward. Watch Episode 5 Meet the team in person 26 August: Fine-tuning the agent stack, London Join Prolific and AI Circle to hear from technical leaders on how teams are fine-tuning agentic systems and evaluating them under real-world conditions. We’ll examine how to design stronger agent harnesses, build evaluations that capture long-horizon behaviour and close the gap between prototypes and dependable systems. Register here . 10 September: A New Era for Data Quality in Online Research, Online With MTurk closing to new customers , a lot of researchers are rethinking how they approach online recruitment and data collection altogether. Join us for a fireside conversation grounded in real evidence. We'll cover an independent, peer-reviewed PLOS ONE study comparing data quality across major research platforms, co-authored by Dr. Andrew Gordon . Register here That's all for our August update! See you next month. The Prolific team

title: Recruiting questions for interviews: Situational, behavior, and role-based
summary: Learn how to ask the right questions in interviews. Explore ready-to-use examples of situational, behavioral, role-based, skill-focused, and cultural questions.
body_text: Most interview question lists enumerate endless examples that look like something you’d conceivably ask in an interview. But what these lists lack (and what interviewers truly need) is questions grouped by what they teach you about the candidate. This guide does exactly that. Below, we’ll break down four types of recruiting questions for interviews: behavioral, situational, role/skills-based, and motivation/culture-add–based questions, explaining what a strong answer sounds like for each. We’ll also walk you through some questions to avoid, and how to turn a question list into a structured interview process guide. How to use interview questions effectively Why use a list of questions for interviews in the first place? Some assume it’s simply to avoid running out of things to say during a screen with someone you’re meeting for the first time. And while it’s never a bad idea to have a conversation starter ready, this answer overlooks the true value of a prepared list of questions: structure. As an interviewer, your goal should be to create as structured of an interview experience across candidates as possible. Asking the same questions every time enables a consistent scoring approach across candidates, which in turn produces fairer comparisons and stronger predictions than what an unstructured chat can provide. The questions below are grouped by what they reveal about the candidate. So make sure to pull from each to build a balanced set when your next position opens. Behavioral interview questions Behavioral questions ask candidates to describe how they reacted to past situations. The value here rests on the assumption that past behavior is predictive of future performance, and it’s usually a pretty safe bet. As the interviewer, listen carefully for specificity, concrete outcomes, and a clear delineation between the candidate’s own actions and collective work done as a group. Sample questions Tell me about a time you disagreed with a manager or peer. How did you handle it? Describe a project that didn’t go the way you planned. What happened next? Tell me about a time you had to influence an outcome owned by someone you had no direct authority over. How did it go? Walk me through the most complex problem you solved in the past year. How did you approach it? Describe a time you were handed a deadline you believed was unrealistic. How did you communicate, and how did the proposal impact the project timeline? What to listen for The strongest answers will describe situations, decision points, and actions with a high level of specificity. There should also be stakes attached to the problem; e.g., meeting client expectations, achieving a difficult KPI, or handling a tough conversation. The explanation should close with a concrete outcome, even if that outcome was undesirable. Encourage the candidate to focus on the actions they personally took. Reluctance or inability to do so is often a red flag. Finally, ask candidates to hone in on a specific instance from the past, avoiding the temptation to speak in broad generalities, or about “how they’d usually handle” X. Situational interview questions Situational questions pose a hypothetical scenario to see how a candidate would approach it. Unlike behavioral questions, situational questions aren’t tethered to first-hand experiences. Instead, they seek to evaluate critical thinking and problem solving skills against an array of potential challenges. These questions work when interviewing candidates at any level of seniority, but are particularly useful when assessing junior candidates who might lack specific, role-relevant experience. Sample questions Imagine you inherit a project that’s already two weeks behind schedule from an owner who’s left the organization. What would you do first? A stakeholder asks you to do something that would push out your current deadline. How do you respond? You notice a mistake in a finalized deliverable that’s already reached a client. What are your next steps? Two leaders on your team give you conflicting priorities. How do you decide between the two? You’re asked to reach a goal, but given no defined process for reaching it. Where do you start? What to listen for The signal you pull out of these questions isn’t necessarily the answer, but the reasoning and thought process that goes into it. Strong candidates will ask questions before deciding on a specific path. They’ll also fluently articulate the tradeoffs between a set of given options. For software engineers, growth strategists, sales reps, and most roles in the broader category of knowledge work, the ability to reason and ask the right questions is more valuable than reflexively running the same playbook across different contexts. Role and skills-based questions Role and skills-based questions probe specific competencies required for success in the role. The exact phrasing of the below examples will depend on the role you’re hiring, but you can apply the framing across different functions and seniority levels. Sample questions Which parts of the project listed on your resume did you personally own, and which were shared with other stakeholders? Walk me through how you would approach [core task of the role] in the first 30, 60, and 90 days. What tools and frameworks do you use for [specific function of the role]? How has your approach evolved in recent years with the arrival of tools like generative AI and agentic workflows? Explain something about [core element of the role] that most people on the outside get wrong. What decision in your last role would you make differently now? What to listen for A primary aim of these questions is to separate verified capabilities from what a candidate’s credentials appear to claim. When candidates struggle to explain what they can do in their own words, it often indicates misalignment with the stated capabilities on their resume. Strong candidates will also be able to clearly explain the parts of projects they owned in their entirety, versus the elements they shared with others. These questions are helpful for making the distinction, especially when interviewing senior candidates whose titles can overstate the scope of their responsibilities. Motivation and culture-add questions Questions in this category seek to surface the reasons a candidate wants this role in particular. They also reveal helpful information about management style and preferences. We advise framing these questions as a matter of “culture-add” versus “culture-fit,” as screening exclusively for candidates who adhere closely to the existing team culture tends to box out those whose perspectives and experiences are different enough to improve decision making quality. Sample questions Why did you decide to apply for this position, specifically? How would you describe your working style? How do you handle receiving feedback? What would you change about the culture of the last team you were a part of? What would you like to be working on that your current or previous position didn’t prioritize? What to listen for True alignment, not just a canned answer. A candidate who takes the time to read about the company, the market it operates in, the job description, or your professional experience before hopping on the call is demonstrating real interest. Questions to avoid As a best practice, employers should avoid questions that aren’t relevant for making a determination about essential job qualifications, especially those touching on personal or protected characteristics. Two categories of questions are explicitly prohibited under federal law. The Americans with Disabilities Act bars potential employers from asking any questions that could reveal a disability before a conditional offer is made. In a similar vein, the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act makes it illegal to ask questions about whether a medical condition runs in the family. Many other sensitive topics aren't criminalized the way ADA and GINA questions are, but that doesn't make them safe. Asking directly about characteristics like race, sex, religion, or national origin is direct evidence of discrimination under Title VII. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission notes that some types of questions could be seen as evidence of discrimination if a candidate you reject later challenges the decision. Avoid questions about the following: Race, color, or ethnicity Sex, gender identity, or sexual orientation Age Family status (including pregnancy and marital status) National origin or citizenship Religion Disability or health Personal associations, especially clubs or organizations that reveal any of the above Note that requirements vary by jurisdiction, and some states’ rules (e.g., asking about salary/compensation history) are more restrictive than the baseline set by the federal government. Check regulations from where you’re hiring first to be sure. Build a structured interview scorecard If you’ve defined a question set, building out a repeatable scorecard to guide the live interview is just a few steps away. Here’s what to do: Choose a consistent question set per role Define what strong answers look like for each question, and give concrete examples Create a scoring scale (e.g., 1–4 or 1–5) and use it across each candidate, with typical behavior for each score characterized in the document The consistency of questions and grading criteria you get from an interview scorecard is what makes the questions predictive of future job success, rather than an anecdotal list of preferences. Better questions start with better candidates The best interview questions only matter if the right people are in the room to answer them. Getting them there? That’s a matter of sourcing effectively. Juicebox is the sourcing layer that fills the pipeline of qualified candidates worth interviewing. Juicebox offers plain-language search that lets recruiters use the same words they get in a Slack from the hiring manager to build a qualified shortlist in minutes, not days. Try a free search today . FAQs What are the best interview questions to ask candidates? The best interview questions to ask candidates are those that are structured to create a consistent, repeatable, and fair set of criteria by which all candidates for the role can be evaluated. Thematically, they touch on behavioral, situational, motivational, cultural, and role-based topics. What is the difference between behavioral and situational questions? Behavioral interview questions probe what candidates did in past situations, hoping to surface concrete evidence of how they handled the biggest challenges in their careers. Situational questions are more geared at understanding how candidates would react to hypothetical contexts, with a focus on understanding what their thought processes and reasoning look like. How many questions should an interview include? For a 45 to 60 minute interview, aim to ask 5 to 8 questions. This allows time for substantive follow-up questions that can provide greater detail. It also leaves time for the candidate to ask their own questions at the end.
